problem: Deep-RL navigation agents had been developed and tested in small or stylized worlds: VizDoom and DeepMind Lab mazes, AI2-THOR's 32 single rooms, CMP's 6 floors. Those settings lack realistic interconnected multi-room layouts, furniture clutter, scale and flexible multimodal sensing. No common benchmark existed to compare such agents on generalization to unseen, realistic indoor environments.
motivation: Training navigation on physical robots is slow, risks damage to the hardware, needs human supervision and cannot cover many environments, so simulation is the practical route. Sim-to-real transfer is more likely to work if the simulator offers many large, realistic 3D scenes. The authors observe that deep-RL agents shown to work in simple mazes have never been fairly compared in large, cluttered, diverse houses. They also note that multimodal perception (depth, touch) matters for animals and agents but is rarely studied in a controlled way.
key_idea: Build a fast (hundreds of FPS), open-source, configurable indoor simulator on top of SUNCG (~45K synthetic houses) and Matterport3D (90 reconstructed buildings), with arbitrary multimodal sensor suites and scene variation. Use it to define fixed-split PointGoal, ObjectGoal and RoomGoal benchmarks that expose how deep-RL navigators degrade with environment size, clutter and realism.
insight: Environment complexity and realism, not the choice of algorithm, dominate performance. The best PointGoal agent reaches 80.3% SR in empty two-room SUNCG houses but at most 20.0% in medium Matterport3D houses (up to 24 rooms), and RoomGoal is harder still (best 14.0% in small Matterport3D scenes), which the authors attribute to its sparse room-type reward. Memory plus auxiliary tasks (UNREAL) matters most in large or semantic settings (58.6 vs 22.5 for DFP on RoomGoal SUNCG-small), while the memory-less DFP wins on small, uncluttered PointGoal. The modality ablation (Table 3) shows depth and contact force are each more useful than grayscale vision; the full depth+vision+force agent is best in furnished houses (48.0 SR vs 30.4 vision-only and 43.7 depth-only), so multimodality helps most under clutter.
method: Simulator architecture: a WebGL rendering server with a client-server design and WebSocket communication. It exposes a Python RL API (OpenAI-Gym style, supports distributed/parallel training) and a web client for interactive and AMT crowdsourced use. Throughput is hundreds of steps/s per workstation (~668 steps/s over 16 threads on one Titan X).

Environment/dataset layer: sources scenes from SUNCG and Matterport3D. Scene selection uses filter predicates (e.g., nrooms==1 && ndoors>0). The benchmark uses a 500-house single-floor SUNCG subset split 300/100/100 with empty and furnished variants, and the official Matterport3D split 61/11/18.

Agent model: a cylinder proxy (height 1.09 m, radius 0.10 m) under rigid-body physics with acceleration-based commands (forward/back, turn, look, strafe). Mass, friction and speed limits are parameterized, giving continuous or effectively discrete control. Experiments discretize actions to forward (~20 cm) and turn left/right (~23°) in a continuous state space.

Generic multimodal sensor API: any number of sensors with configurable position, orientation, resolution and encoding. Available types are RGB/grayscale, depth (with optional noise model), surface normals, semantic/instance segmentation, contact-force sensors, and measurements (velocity, Euclidean/geodesic distance and direction to goal, normalized episode time).

Customization: semantically consistent retexturing that respects the train/val/test splits, object-clutter control (removing chosen categories), goal specification (point, object category, room category; any/random/closest instance), and task/reward definition as an arbitrary Python function.

Benchmark tasks: PointGoal (Euclidean distance plus normalized direction to the goal), RoomGoal (one-hot over 9 room classes) and ObjectGoal (doors). Episodes time out at 500 steps (50 s), and start-goal pairs are checked for navigability with a tile-based shortest path. Training uses 10 trials per environment before switching.

Benchmarked agents: A3C-FF, A3C-LSTM, UNREAL and DFP, each trained for 13.2M steps with epsilon-greedy decay to ~10%. The reward is the change in Euclidean goal distance and normalized time; DFP uses measurements ⟨d, x, z, t⟩ with offsets 1–32 steps. Multimodal DFP variants add GT depth and 4 binary contact sensors to the 84×84 grayscale input.

setting.backbone: Existing deep-RL agents trained from scratch in MINOS: A3C-FF, A3C-LSTM, UNREAL (conv nets ± LSTM) and DFP (Direct Future Prediction); multimodal study uses DFP
setting.training_data: Online RL in MINOS, 13.2M simulation steps per agent (~15 days simulated experience). Uses 300 SUNCG training houses (from a 500-house single-floor subset, empty/furnished variants) or the 61 Matterport3D training scenes. No external data.
setting.observation: Egocentric 84×84 grayscale camera (90° FOV, height 1.09 m) + goal signal (GT Euclidean distance and normalized direction for PointGoal/ObjectGoal; one-hot room class for RoomGoal). Multimodal variants add noise-free GT depth (0–10 m, byte-quantized) and 4 binary contact-force sensors.
setting.action_space: Discretized {move forward, turn left, turn right} applied as accelerations (20 m/s², 4π rad/s²) in a continuous-state physics sim, ≈20 cm steps and ≈23° turns; 500-step episode limit
setting.privileged: GT Euclidean distance and direction to the goal (point, or closest point of goal object) given every step, via a perfect indoor-GPS-like signal. Depth is ground truth and noise-free. The DFP RoomGoal measurement uses whether the current room category matches the goal.

numbers_note: This is a simulator/benchmark paper with no novel navigation method. All entries are existing RL agents (DFP, UNREAL; also A3C-FF and A3C-LSTM, omitted here) trained and evaluated by the authors in MINOS; there are no numbers on canonical later benchmarks. The split is inferred as 'test' from 'tested on novel environments' (the paper defines train/val/test splits but does not name the evaluation split explicitly). The Size/Clutter conditions (Small = 2-room SUNCG or ≤10-room Matterport3D; Medium = 3–5-room SUNCG or ≤24-room Matterport3D) are subsets of the evaluation scenes. Table 2 also reports Random, A3C-FF and A3C-LSTM rows. Table 3 also has None, Measurements, M+Depth (e.g., 43.7/28.5 furnished house), M+Forces, M+V+F and Human (99.0–100.0 SR) rows. The success-distance threshold is not stated.
results: Deep-RL agents degrade sharply with scale, clutter and realism. On PointGoal, DFP reaches 80.3% SR in empty two-room SUNCG houses, but every agent is ≤20% in medium Matterport3D houses (UNREAL 20.0). On RoomGoal the best is 58.6 (UNREAL, SUNCG small) and only 14.0 in small Matterport3D scenes. UNREAL is best overall in large and semantic settings, DFP is best in small uncluttered scenes, and A3C-FF fails to learn. In the door-ObjectGoal multimodal study, the full depth+vision+force DFP agent is best in furnished houses (48.0 SR vs 30.4 vision-only, 43.7 depth-only), yet remains far below humans (99.0).
limitations: Only off-the-shelf model-free RL agents with borrowed hyperparameters and 13.2M steps are benchmarked (A3C-FF may have failed due to hyperparameters). No map-based or classical baselines are included; CMP was excluded because it assumes a gridworld.
Agents receive a perfect GT goal distance/direction signal and noise-free GT depth. ObjectGoal is evaluated only with doors as targets. Human performance is measured on only one episode per scene.
Sim-to-real transfer is claimed as motivation but not validated. SUNCG was later withdrawn, and Matterport3D results cover only small and medium subsets (no RoomGoal/ObjectGoal on large scenes).
